extracted.intended_audience: general literate public (early-18th-century readers interested in manners, conversation, and wit), especially genteel men and women
extracted.subtask_description: Short, prescriptive essays and letters offering advice and standards for social behaviour, conversation, courage, aging, and the practical arts of being agreeable (especially how men should comport themselves to please women and to command).

rubrics_metrics.name: Man of Pleasure — character and consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: A man whose chief character is pleasure is 'a negligent Friend, Father, and Husband' and 'entails Poverty on his unhappy Descendants'; mortgages, diseases, and settlements are his legacies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay warns that devotion to immediate delight sacrifices duty and long-term happiness: such a man loses the delicacy of his passions to appetites, fails in serious offices of life, and leaves his family in poverty. Examples/notes: 'Mortgages Diseases, and Settlements are the Legacies a Man of Wit and Pleasure leaves to his Family.' Anti-pattern: pursuing 'jollity' at the cost of responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure blinds to its own harms
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasure appears attractive in the moment ('warm Wishes, gay Looks, and graceful Motion') but departs leaving 'Disorder, Impotence, down-cast Shame, and conscious Imperfection'; it 'makes our Youth inglorious, our Age shameful.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that transient gratifications conceal lasting losses of self-respect and dignity. The text uses vivid contrasts to show the immediate allure versus the long-term damage; anti-pattern is valuing only the approach of pleasure without attending to its aftermath.

rubrics_metrics.name: Talent can make vice seem tolerable
rubrics_metrics.description: Because 'some Men of great Talents have sacrificed themselves to' pleasure, their shining qualities have 'given a Beauty to whatever they were engaged in, and a Mixture of Wit has recommended Madness.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author cautions against excusing bad behaviour simply because a person is witty or talented; applause for the entertaining aspects can mask impertinence, cruelty, or irresponsibility. Example: celebrated wits whose follies were tolerated; anti-pattern: using fame or cleverness as a shield for vice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical courage vs. reasoned command
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a 'Mechanick Courage' learned by acting always in a crowd (men who march into breaches with alacrity), distinct from the courage of commanders who have 'reasoned themselves... into such a Negligence of their Being.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between habit-driven bravery (crowd-bred, indifferent to risk) and the higher courage of leaders who, by reflection and duty, accept the danger of death in pursuit of a greater good. The latter requires resignation to mortality and a sense of conscience and duty; anti-pattern: confusing mere reckless habit for true heroic leadership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities of a worthy commander
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaders are those who put duty and the greater good above length of days, draw resolution from the impossibility of escape, and inspire mutual love and readiness to risk among their men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good commander is just, modest, and beloved: he distributes rewards fairly, behaves humbly (would think himself 'below their Tailor' to wear a snip of lace), and creates a band where 'every Man [is] afraid for himself and his Neighbour' out of affection rather than fear of punishment. This produces true mutual courage and devotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Military life erodes ordinary affections
rubrics_metrics.description: Habitual exposure to danger and the crowded life of soldiery can produce indifference: companions may respond to a drowning friend with 'Ay, he had a mad Horse' rather than grief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essays illustrate how constant danger and communal focus can blunt private tenderness and pity. This is an explanatory criterion for evaluating the emotional effects of a life spent in continual hazard; anti-pattern: mistaking stoic indifference for nobility of character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wishing to be younger is a mark of folly
rubrics_metrics.description: Of all impertinent wishes, none is more unworthy than wishing oneself younger; wanting youth merely for bodily strength or to repeat follies is absurd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues it's irrational and dishonourable for an educated person to lament age in itself: age brings greater reason, refined pleasures, authority, and certain satisfactions (memory of a well-spent youth). Anti-patterns include libidinous old men fretting at nature's course or longing only for the physical capacities of youth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value and pleasures of old age
rubrics_metrics.description: Rational and worthy pleasures (good fame, contemplation, respect of honest men) are enlarged by years; age in a virtuous person carries an authority preferable to the pleasures of youth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay positions mature delights—peace of mind, reputation, contemplative pleasures—as superior and more stable than the feverish dreams of youth. Practical implication: cultivate virtues early to enjoy dignified old age; example quote: 'He that would be long an old Man, must begin early to be one.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Resign youthful pursuits before age arrives
rubrics_metrics.description: It is necessary that before the Arrival of Age we bid adieu to the Pursuits of Youth, otherwise sensual Habits will live in our Imaginations when our Limbs cannot be subservient to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical counsel: abandon sensual habits while still able to avoid them, so that later physical decline won't produce irrational desires or misery. Example anecdote: the soldier who lost an arm still feels his buried fingers ache. Anti-pattern: clinging to youthful licence into old age.

rubrics_metrics.name: How young men should cultivate presence to please women
rubrics_metrics.description: Young men of good education 'take too little Care of improving themselves in little things: A good Air at entring into a Room, a proper Audacity in expressing himself with Gaiety and Gracefulness' would make a young Gentleman of Virtue and Sense capable of discountenancing the shallow impudent Rogues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete behavioural skills (entrance, bearing, audacity balanced with grace) are recommended as tactics to be socially successful and to stand out against more impudent rivals. Example: Simon Honeycomb's deliberate reinvention—changing scene, adopting an impudent face—to win favour; anti-pattern: passive modesty leading to social dismissal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attributes of the successful 'Woman's Man' (how to be a favourite)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Woman's Man dresses loose and negligent, has a soft indolent manner, imitates the creature he hopes to betray, is officious in small services, keeps a bottle for sudden indisposition, has singular behaviour that would make him ridiculous among men, and must have reputation for being 'well with other Women.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay catalogues stylized traits that attract the fair sex: singularity of behaviour, wit and humour, a reputation for inconstancy (which paradoxically pleases), the art of preventing explanation among rivals, and spiteful charm. It also notes that men of true sense are rarely general favourites. This is both descriptive and prescriptive of courtship tactics; anti-pattern: trying to win women by sober good sense alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversational entertainment valued above sober judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: In the mating-market of conversation, 'it is much better to have a Faculty of arguing, than a Capacity of judging right.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author advises that the ability to entertain, argue, and keep lively discourse is more socially rewarded (particularly with women) than mere good judgment. Implication for social performance: cultivate repartee and spirited talk; anti-pattern: being silent or only judicious, which may be read as dullness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decency in public speech toward women and commercial consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Tradeswomen and public-house keepers suffer 'immodest Discourses' and ribaldry from customers who force such talk on them; this affront is 'out of all Decency' and harms their business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Letters in the paper urge readers (gentlemen) to desist from making immodest jokes in the hearing of women at counters or bars, since such behaviour insults modesty, drives away customers, and may lead to economic ruin. Proposed remedies include public shaming (writing down offenders) or encouraging gentlemen to show proper deference. Anti-pattern: treating a modest working woman as if she 'knows as well as we' and thereby trivializing her position.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flirtation and idle admirers can ruin a woman's livelihood
rubrics_metrics.description: A milliner reports that admirers 'tumble over all my Goods' and ogle for entertainment, buying little while occupying time; being treated 'for nothing but my Beauty' threatens her trade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay points out the practical harm of frivolous flirtation: it displaces serious customers and risks a tradeswoman's business. Humorous/proposed remedies (from the letter) include 'assign Rates to my kind Glances, or make all pay who come to see me'—i.e., regulate or monetize attention. Use this as a social-economical criterion when judging public decorum.
